summary: Defines a mechanism based on a new STUN usage that obtains periodic consent from a remote endpoint to keep sending traffic. This prevents WebRTC applications such as browsers from being used to attack unwilling victims.

eli5.summary: Before you keep throwing a ball at someone, you keep asking 'still okay?' so you never hit someone who does not want to play.

questions: how does webrtc prevent traffic attacks
how often are webrtc consent checks sent
how long does webrtc consent last
subtitle: How a WebRTC endpoint keeps checking that the other side still wants its traffic, every few seconds, or stops sending.

tldr.problem: A malicious script in a browser could use the browser to send traffic at a victim that never agreed to receive it, and ICE only checks consent once, when the session starts.
tldr.mechanism: The sender keeps sending STUN binding requests to the peer and needs a valid authenticated response; if none arrives within 30 seconds, it must stop sending on that 5-tuple.
tldr.outcome: Consent now has a built-in expiry, so a peer that goes quiet or says no (for example with a 403 Forbidden error) cuts off the traffic. RFC 7675 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7675 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Consent Must Be Renewed
sections.content:
Endpoints have to make sure the remote peer is willing to receive traffic. In deployments like WebRTC this matters because a malicious JavaScript program must not be able to use the browser as a platform for launching attacks.

Consent is first obtained when a session is set up, through ICE connectivity checks (RFC 5245). This RFC adds the second half: a new STUN usage that keeps checking, for the whole life of the session, that the peer still consents. Consent expires after a period of time and has to be continually renewed, which ensures that consent can be terminated.

Consent applies to a single 5-tuple. How an application reacts when consent changes is not described here, and the mechanism does not update the ICE procedures.
sections.eli5: Getting a yes once is not enough. You keep checking that the answer is still yes, so you can stop if it changes to no.

sections.title: Who This Applies To
sections.content:
Only full ICE implementations obtain consent this way. An ICE-lite agent does not generate connectivity checks, so it does not generate consent checks either. It only answers the ones it receives, and since those are processed as normal ICE connectivity checks, no changes are required to ICE-lite implementations.

Other applications with similar needs, such as verifying consent before sending non-ICE packets, can reuse the mechanism. How an application learns that consent has expired is outside the scope of the document.

The document defines consent as permission from the remote endpoint to send non-ICE traffic to a remote transport address, and notes that this is application-level: no human intervention is involved.
sections.eli5: Only players who actually run the whole game ask the questions. A helper who just answers does not need to learn anything new.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
ICE already sends keepalives to hold NAT bindings open, but those are STUN Indications: send-and-forget messages that get no response. Consent needs a response, so a request/response exchange is required. ICE endpoints already have to keep listening for ICE messages, so ICE is a natural carrier.

The STUN binding requests used for consent also keep NAT bindings alive. For that reason dedicated keepalives such as Binding Indications are not sent on candidate pairs where consent requests are sent.

The RFC also explains why a valid SRTP packet is not enough proof of consent. With two parties, an authenticated packet is strong assurance it came from the other party. When more than two parties share keys, any of them could have sent or spoofed it. The mechanism is an optional extension to ICE and can be deployed at one end of a two-party session without impact on the other party.
sections.eli5: A friend waving once in a while is not the same as a friend answering your question. You need an answer back, so you ask a real question.

sections.title: How Consent Expires and Is Renewed
sections.content:
An endpoint gains consent to send on a candidate pair when the pair enters the Succeeded ICE state. The expiry time is 30 seconds, chosen to balance a quick reaction to lost consent against spurious failures. An endpoint MUST NOT send data other than the messages used to establish consent until the receiver has consented, so no application data (RTP or DTLS, for example) goes out first.

Consent is maintained by sending a STUN binding request to the peer's transport address and receiving a matching, authenticated, non-error binding response. These messages use the same short-term credentials as the initial ICE exchange. If no valid response arrives within 30 seconds, the endpoint MUST cease transmission on that 5-tuple. A response after expiry does not re-establish consent.

Requests are sent periodically. Each interval MUST be randomized between 0.8 and 1.2 times the basic period, to prevent synchronization of checks. Implementations SHOULD default to 5 seconds, giving 4 to 6 seconds between checks, and MUST NOT go below 4 seconds. Every request uses a new transaction identifier and is sent once only, so a response might belong to an earlier request.

Consent checks are required over TCP too. TCP has its own acknowledgements, but a TCP connection could be translated to UDP, and an off-path attacker could spoof ACKs to make a sender keep sending.

After consent is lost, the same ICE credentials MUST NOT be used on that 5-tuple again; a new session or an ICE restart is needed. An endpoint that keeps sending on the old pair during an ICE restart MUST keep doing consent freshness on it. An endpoint that sends no application data does not need to maintain consent, but MUST regain it before it resumes.
sections.eli5: Every few seconds you ask 'still okay?'. If you hear nothing back for half a minute, you stop. Once you have stopped, you must start over with a new introduction.

sections.title: Revoking Consent Immediately
sections.content:
Waiting for a timeout is sometimes too slow. Consent for sending application data is revoked at once by an authenticated message that closes the connection (for example a TLS fatal alert) or by a valid, authenticated STUN response with error code 403 (Forbidden). Since such messages can be lost, an endpoint could resend them or simply wait for consent to expire.

Unauthenticated signals do not count. A message like a TCP FIN that closes a connection does not revoke consent, so the receiver SHOULD keep sending media (over connectionless transport) or try to re-establish the connection (over connection-oriented transport) until consent expires or an authenticated revocation arrives. An authenticated SRTCP BYE does not end consent either; it only says the SRTP source has quit.
sections.eli5: If someone clearly and truthfully says 'stop', you stop right away. A stranger shouting 'stop' for them does not count.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The transaction ID must be hard to guess. Consent requires the 96-bit transaction ID from RFC 5389 to be uniformly and randomly chosen from 0 .. 2**96-1 and to be cryptographically strong. The RFC calls this good enough against an off-path attacker replaying old STUN consent responses.

Untrusted application code, such as JavaScript or signaling servers, MUST NOT be able to obtain or control the STUN transaction identifier, because that would enable spoofing of responses and falsified consent.

The RFC points to the WebRTC security documents for the browser-as-attack-platform discussion, and says the security considerations of RFC 5245 should also be taken into account. DTLS applicability is identical to Section 4.2 of RFC 7350, and consent checks SHOULD use the same Diffserv markings as ICE connectivity checks for a given 5-tuple.
sections.eli5: The 'still okay?' note has a secret random number on it, so nobody can fake a reply, and the script on the web page is not allowed to see that number.

viz.caption: WHAT ENDS CONSENT, AND WHAT DOES NOT

items.title: 403 Forbidden
items.text: Authenticated STUN error response revokes consent at once.

items.title: Authenticated close
items.text: For example a TLS fatal alert.

items.title: Not enough
items.text: A TCP FIN or an SRTCP BYE does not revoke consent.
